I can see no sufficient reason for doubting that in the Fragments as printed we have, as Bolingbroke asserted, in a somewhat expanded form “the notes which were communicated to Mr. Pope in scraps, as they were written,” and utilized by the latter in writing the Essay on Man; the numerous and exact verbal parallels between passages in the Fragments and the Essay are not susceptible of any other probable explanation (see Bolingbroke’s Works, 1809 ed., VII, 278, and VIII, 356). Law wrote in the preface to the 1781 edition of the Essay on the Origin of Evil: “I had the satisfaction of seeing that those very principles which had been maintained by Archbishop King were adopted by Mr. Pope in the Essay on Man.” When this was challenged by a brother-bishop, Pope’s truculent theological champion Warburton, Law replied by referring to the testimony of Lord Bathurst, “who saw the very same system in Lord Bolingbroke’s own hand, lying before Mr. Pope while he composed his Essay”; and added: “The point may also be cleared effectively whenever any reader shall think it worth his while to compare the two pieces together, and observe how exactly they tally with one another” (op. cit., p. xvii). Such a comparison seems to me to give reason to believe that Pope made use of King’s work directly, as well as of Bolingbroke’s adaptation of a part of it. Since it was in 1730 that Pope and Bolingbroke were “deep in metaphysics,” and since by 1731 the first three Epistles seem to have been completed (cf. Courthope, V, 242), it must have been from the Latin original, not Law’s translation, that the poet and his philosophic mentor drew. Thus essentially the same theodicy appeared almost simultaneously in Law’s English prose rendering and in Pope’s verse. parsing_res_list.block_content: ### THE LOEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY

The great literature of the Greeks and Romans has remained alive throughout the centuries because of the deeply satisfying pleasure it has given to each new generation of readers. The Odyssey of Homer, the poems of Ovid, the philosophy of Plato, the adventures of Aeneas—these are old friends of the classroom. But many other books, by both familiar and less well-known authors, provide reading as stimulating today as it was two thousand years ago. The witty dialogues of Lucian, the brilliant comedies of Aristophanes, the travels of Strabo, and the botanical discoveries of Theophrastus, founder of modern botany, are only samples of the wide range of subjects included in the LoEB CLASSICAL LIBRARY of over 450 titles. Studies in the Decay of Christian Humanism in the

Earlier Seventeenth Century
BY HERSCHEL BAKER

"Prof. Baker's admirable 'The Dignity of Man,' which analyzed western man's philosophical and literary estimate of himself in the cosmic scheme up to and including the Renaissance, now has an equally entrancing sequel in 'The Wars of Truth,' which closes this series of studies. 'The Wars of Truth' brings the revolution down to understandable dimension. The author's urbane and scholarly style makes this book, like its predecessor, a joy to read."—Boston Traveler. "Very fully documented, this study will be of great interest to the historian of ideas and to the specialist in the literature, philosophy, and theology of the seventeenth century."—The United States Quarterly Book Review. $6.00
### STUDIES IN THE PHILOSOPHY OF CHARLES SANDERS PEIRCE
EDITED BY PHILIP P. WIENER AND FREDERIC H. YOUNG

"Twenty-five able scholars [including Arthur O. Lovejoy] have contributed to this distinguished collection of essays on the philosophy of Peirce. The subjects covered include all aspects of Peirce's thought and fall into four main groups: the pragmaticist theory of meaning; the philosophy of common sense, science and logic; speculations in phenomenology, metaphysics, and the philosophy of religion; and biographical and historical researches on Peirce. Among other things, the five appendixes present hitherto unpublished letters on Peirce at Johns Hopkins and additions to the Peirce bibliography. ... The contributors pay him the compliment not of worship but of taking his ideas seriously. The result is a contribution to the understanding of knowledge and its methods, and of reality and its structure, that should interest every student of philosophy and of American culture."—The United States Quarterly Book Review.
